extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, Patent Office examiners, and inventors dealing with re-issue/amendment of patents
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evidentiary principles for determining what may be claimed in a re-issued patent and how courts/Patent Office ascertain the invention the patentee originally intended to describe and protect. Covers limitations (no new matter), sources of evidence, machine-patent special rules, presumptions of validity, and when extrinsic evidence is admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue limited to what was intended in original patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is entitled to claim in his re-issue only what he 'intended to' describe and claim in his original patent; a re-issue is intended to cover the invention which the inventor actually made and attempted to protect by the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Patent Office will not permit a re-issue to claim subject-matter that the inventor did not attempt to describe and claim in the original patent; many cases cited illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: No attempt in original bars inclusion in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: If no attempt was made to secure the invention by the original patent, it cannot be embraced in a re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the original specification/drawings/model show no effort to claim an invention, the re-issue cannot legitimately expand to cover that matter (cases: Hoskin v. Fisher, Marsh v. Seymour referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot claim a different or broader invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot claim either another invention or a broader invention than the one attempted to be described and claimed in the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in a re-issue that enlarge the invention beyond what was attempted in the original are invalid; compare original and re-issue instruments to determine scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibition of new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1870 Act (and Revised Statutes) provide 'no new matter shall be introduced into the specification, nor, in case of a machine-patent, shall the model or drawings be amended except each by the other; but, when there is neither model nor drawing, amendments may be made upon proof satisfactory to the Commissioner that such new matter or amendment was part of the original invention and was omitted...by inadvertence, accident, or mistake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory rule limits re-issue amendments: new matter is prohibited unless proven to have been part of the original invention and omitted by mistake; for machines, drawings/models tie amendments together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original specification/drawings/model are primary test
rubrics_metrics.description: The original specification, as illustrated by the model or drawings if any, and as interpreted by proper explanation and examination, must bear upon its face sufficient evidence of the alleged endeavor to describe and claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office and courts rely primarily on the original patent instruments to determine what the inventor attempted to claim; extrinsic assertions are subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: When original specification is defective, examine the actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification is confessedly defective (inoperative or invalid), mere interpretation cannot cure it; the actual invention as made and practiced must be examined to discover what the inventor intended and attempted to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original disclosure is inadequate, the Patent Office or courts may look beyond the paper to the inventor's actual device/model and other evidence to measure the defect and intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sources of information for intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Three sources may bear on the actual character of the original invention: (1) assertions of the inventor (parol testimony); (2) the specification of the re-issued patent; (3) the invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources are used in varying degrees. The re-issue specification (when filed) and the invention itself are authoritative; parol testimony is generally excluded or treated with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue specification (when perfected) is authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: When the re-issue application is perfected and the applicant insists it corresponds with the actual invention as originally secured, the specification, drawings, and model in the re-issue become the test by which the intended scope of the original patent is to be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once perfected, the re-issue specification gives a complete and exact description of the invention as the inventor now asserts it and furnishes a ready, permanent standard against which the original may be compared; extrinsic testimony is largely excluded thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol testimony mostly inadmissible to expand scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Parol testimony (inventor's assertions) is unreliable and unnecessary when the re-issue specification is available, and is not admissible in an application for a re-issue to enlarge the scope beyond what was described, suggested, or substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of surrender and re-issue is to render effectual the actual invention, not to introduce new features by parol evidence; courts exclude parol to prevent fraud and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: If original description is complete, extrinsic inquiry unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the description of the original patent is complete and accurate, and the fault resides only in an obscure, too restricted, or excessive claim, the original description becomes the standard and exterior evidence or examination of the actual invention is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the Patent Office/courts should judge and correct claim imperfections by reference to the original specification/drawings/model alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue must not introduce interpolations of new features
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolations in a re-issued patent of new features or ingredients or devices which were neither described, suggested, nor substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or Patent Office model are not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A re-issue cannot be used to add novel matter; its function is remedial—to render the originally made invention effectual—not to expand it with newly conceived elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for original that fails to describe real invention is a new application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the original patent does not describe the real invention, the remedy is by a new application and patent, not by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor truly failed to disclose the actual inventive subject-matter at all, re-issue is not the proper vehicle to secure that subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity from issuance but courts may re-examine
rubrics_metrics.description: The issuance of a patent raises a presumption of its validity and the existence of statutory conditions, which could justify treating the Patent Office allowance as final; later cases, however, show the courts will re-examine and not treat allowance as conclusively conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare original and re-issue specifications affirmatively; courts have varied between deferring to Office allowance and re-evaluating validity by closer comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of instruments is the operative test
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the inventor's original attempt and the subject-matter in the re-issue is to be ascertained by comparing the original specification/drawings/model with those of the re-issue; if the instruments show it on their faces, no extrinsic evidence is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If from mere comparison the inventions appear different, the question of identity may be one of construction (law) for the court; if not apparent, factual inquiry (jury) may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-patent special rule: model/drawings presumed to show intended features
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a machine-patent it is assumed that every feature of the invention which the inventor intended to protect will be exhibited either in his drawing or his model, and by prescribing that these can be amended only by each other the statute implies that no part of the actual invention can be regarded as embraced unless disclosed in one or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machine patents the drawings/model have heightened evidentiary importance; amendments to one must be reflected in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue that contains only claims not in original may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue whose only claims are not in the original is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that if the re-issue adds claims entirely absent from the original disclosure, the re-issued patent may be invalid; however, nuances and exceptions (e.g., claims that were impliedly suggested) exist in case law.
